text.en: Can a young violinist play Indo-Western fusion and still respect her father's classical tradition? This play shows how a family finds harmony.

The characters are Shruti Sharma, a young violinist; her father Guru Nabin Sharma, a violinist and principal of the Sangeetika Music School; her mother Leela Devi; and her band friends Avinash (tabla), Iqbal (flute) and Peter (keyboard).
Act I is set in Iqbal's room after a fusion rehearsal. A newspaper has praised Shruti's performance with her father, but she looks distressed because she has not told her father about the fusion concert.
Shruti explains that her father is strict and believes only classical Hindustani music with ragas and alaaps is worthy. She does not want to disrespect his opinion but wants to try fusion too.
Her friends encourage her to speak up, and she promises to tell him at dinner.
In Act II, over dinner, Shruti tells her father about an Indo-Western fusion concert. He refuses calmly but firmly, saying one performance every six months is his rule and that fusion makes the violinist lose musicality.
Later Shruti's parents come to her rehearsal. Her mother Leela reminds Nabin of his own past: his family were classical vocalists and his father saw his choice of a Western instrument, the violin, as a betrayal of family tradition.
Nabin admits he had forgotten his past and that he underestimated the power of Indian music. He promises to support Shruti's group at the concert.
The play shows that tradition and change can live together, and that listening and courage can bring families closer. Twin melodies means two kinds of music in harmony.

problem.en: Why does Shruti hesitate to tell her father about the concert?

text.en: Her father believes only classical music is worthwhile.
She does not want to hurt or disrespect him.

prompt.en: How does the play show that tradition and change can coexist?

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all fusion music disrespects tradition

points.en: Shruti plays fusion and respects classical music.
Leela reminds him of his own past.
The play teaches openness between generations.
